items.title: OneDrop Storage and Multi-Device Sync (Part One)
items.content_html:
My introduction to OneDrop covers the project, installation and future plans. This two-part series looks at the implementation. Here I’ll follow Microsoft account authorisation and the path a text or file message takes through storage, upload and download. Part two covers multi-device sync, conflicts, archives, deletion and recovery.

Using OneDrive saves me from deploying and maintaining a storage service. It still leaves the client responsible for message state. Two devices can edit the same record, an upload can finish before its message commits, and a deletion has to reach other devices. This diagram shows the entry points, shared UI and storage in OneDrop 1.0.3.

# Microsoft accounts and OneDrive authorisation

# The client authorisation flow

OneDrop queries, reads and writes OneDrive files through Microsoft’s API, Microsoft Graph. Both the Edge extension and the standalone iOS app run on the user’s device. Microsoft handles login and file requests. Here “extension” refers specifically to the browser distribution; “client” includes the native app as well.

# Authorisation with PKCE

Requests go directly from the client, so the first step is to get the user’s authorisation. A distributed extension or app can’t keep a server secret confidential. OneDrop uses the authorisation code flow with PKCE. The user signs in and grants consent on Microsoft’s page, then the client exchanges an authorisation code for tokens.

The client generates a random verifier , hashes it with SHA-256 and Base64URL-encodes the digest as a challenge . The authorisation request sends the challenge . The token request later supplies the original verifier alongside the code. The server checks that the digest matches the challenge from this authorisation. Possession of the code alone is insufficient to complete that exchange.

The 64 in the code is the byte count before encoding. The request declares code_challenge_method=S256 . A separate random state is returned unchanged in the callback, allowing the client to match the response to its login attempt. Missing code, mismatched state or an authorisation error stops the exchange.

# Registering the application and setting its configuration

For a custom build, register an application in Microsoft Entra. Entra is where Microsoft manages sign-in and authorisation settings. Registration identifies the application requesting sign-in. Released builds already contain their application configuration; users sign in with their own accounts.

The client needs three settings.

  • Client ID identifies the application. In Entra ID → App registrations, create or open the application and copy Application (client) ID from Overview. This identifies the registration, independently of the user’s account or password.
  • Authority selects the sign-in endpoint and account audience. OneDrop defaults to https://login.microsoftonline.com/common . To support work, school and personal Microsoft accounts, the registration must also allow those account types; select the multitenant option that includes personal accounts.
  • Redirect URI tells Microsoft where to return the result. Register it under Authentication. The URI sent in the request must match. This is a client callback address, unrelated to OneDrive’s file directories.

Desktop Edge supplies extension identity APIs for generating the callback, opening an authorisation window and receiving its result. Android Edge also uses an extension callback but may fail to create the window. In the implementation described here, iOS Edge lacks Identity API and needs a web callback.

When available, browser.identity.getRedirectURL("auth") returns an address such as https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/auth . Before a client ID is configured, OneDrop’s setup screen displays the Redirect URI to register. Copy it from your own installed extension; different packages can have different IDs.

Without that API, the default web callback is https://onedrop.sycamore.top/auth.html , registered as a single-page application (SPA). If you host another callback, change both the local configuration and the Entra registration.

Set the build values in .env.local at the project root:

Restart the development server and reload the extension after editing. Microsoft documents app registration and client account audiences.

# Requesting permissions

OneDrop includes the following scopes in its login request:

  • openid requests identity information so the client can obtain an ID token .
  • profile requests basic profile details such as the name and username shown in the UI.
  • offline_access requests a refresh token so an expired access token can be replaced without another interactive login. OneDrive still requires network access.
  • Files.ReadWrite requests file access on behalf of the signed-in user. Add it under API permissions → Add a permission → Microsoft Graph → Delegated permissions. The application acts as the user rather than independently of one.

Microsoft defines the scopes and the user or organisation must grant them. See the OpenID Connect scope documentation. The delegated file permission extends beyond Apps/OneDrop . The application confines its normal operations to that directory through its own code; creating a folder doesn’t narrow an already granted permission.

# Login windows and session state

# Authorisation window or temporary tab

Desktop Edge prefers browser.identity.launchWebAuthFlow , with a callback from getRedirectURL("auth") . If that API is absent or reports that it cannot create a browser window, OneDrop opens a temporary tab instead. Register the callback actually used by the build.

When launchWebAuthFlow is unavailable, the client persists state , verifier , callback and start time. On a later status check it can see whether the tab reached the callback and finish the exchange.

Interactive login allows the user to act in the sign-in window. Silent login tries to reuse an existing session. Pending authorisation data is retained for five minutes; interactive login waits five minutes and silent login thirty seconds. These limits govern a login attempt, independently of the lifetime of the resulting access token .

# Token roles and storage

The access token authorises Graph requests, the refresh token obtains new access tokens, and the ID token carries identity claims. The extension stores its tokens in browser.storage.local : closing the sidebar can leave the background runtime suspended, so it must be possible to resume without a permanently running process. Native iOS uses Keychain, as described in the platform notes.

# Refreshing tokens and signing in again

getCurrentAccessToken() checks validity before Graph access, allowing a 60-second expiry margin. As expiry approaches, it uses the refresh token to request a new access token . The refreshInFlight ??= in the screenshot lets concurrent callers share that refresh Promise . That avoids duplicate refresh requests and races when saving the responses. The promise is cleared on completion so a future refresh can start.

Ordinary refresh failures return an error. For errors such as invalid_grant or interaction_required , OneDrop first tries silent authorisation with prompt=none . If that also cannot proceed it clears its stored tokens and requests login. Signing out of OneDrop clears its own tokens without signing the browser out of Microsoft.

The UI decodes name and username using readUnverifiedIdTokenClaims . As the name indicates, it reads the fields without verifying the signature locally. These values supply display information, and the username can serve as a silent-login login_hint .

# The Apps/OneDrop directory

Messages, attachments and settings live in one predictable location visible to the user in OneDrive. After obtaining a token the client checks /me/drive/root:/Apps/OneDrop , relative to the signed-in user’s drive root. A 404 indicates a missing directory. It checks and creates each level as needed, first Apps , then OneDrop . Creation fails on conflict; if another device created the folder first, the client rereads it rather than replacing the object. Overwriting an object with the same name could destroy content the other device had already written. Part two uses similar reasoning for writes and archives.

# Storing and transferring text and files

# Separating metadata from attachments

# Cloud layout

Text and files appear in the same message list but are stored differently in OneDrive. Text is small enough to store in JSON. File contents are uploaded separately; their message records store what’s needed to locate and display them. Here’s the layout, using example years and months:

messages contains active chunks, archive holds consolidated months and files contains attachments. Device settings have separate documents under settings , avoiding a shared rewrite for every preference change. Reads use the ID markers in tombstones to filter deleted messages. UTC month boundaries keep devices in different time zones from assigning the same timestamp to different months.

# Message fields and validation

OneDrop uses Zod to define the message schema and validate the JSON it actually reads. TypeScript types alone can’t check an incoming document. The common fields are the format version schemaVersion , a UUID message identifier id , the creation time createdAt and an optional senderDeviceId . Stable IDs identify the original across retries and merges. The sender device ID distinguishes messages from this installation from messages sent on other devices. It identifies an installation, not the Microsoft account.

Text extends the common fields:

The text is trimmed, must remain nonempty and is limited to 20,000 characters. File messages include attachment.driveItemId , filename, size and MIME type, with optional image dimensions and thumbHash . A DriveItem represents a Graph file or folder; a MIME type such as image/png describes its content. The UI can show the name, size and an image placeholder before fetching the object by ID.

Each chunk has its own schemaVersion , month and messages array. Both the chunk and its individual records are validated when read. Users can edit, move or damage files outside OneDrop. Writing a file once doesn’t guarantee it will still match the schema when OneDrop reads it again.

For images the client tries to read the original dimensions and generate a ThumbHash, a compact encoding of a blurred preview. It prefers createImageBitmap , falls back to a local image object, scales proportionally to a longest side of at most 100 pixels and reads RGBA from a temporary canvas. Only the preview canvas is downscaled. The original attachment is uploaded unchanged. If metadata extraction fails the send continues without the optional preview.

# Local pending tasks

Draft text, files waiting to upload, commit state and attachment details needed for retries have to survive a closed UI or a suspended Manifest V3 service worker. OneDrop saves pending text and pending transfer records in IndexedDB, the browser’s local database. A Blob holds the file bytes for retries.

putPendingTransfer() writes a record, getPendingTransfer() retrieves one by ID, and listPendingTransfers() lists them by creation time.

Pending state records work this device still owes. The cloud represents what other devices should see. The UI can show progress early, but sending finishes only after the cloud steps succeed. A retry keeps the message ID so it can recognise an earlier successful commit.

# Sending a file

files/send registers a placeholder, uploads the attachment and then replaces the placeholder with the final file message. The placeholder has type file-uploading and a pendingAttachment , without a final DriveItem ID. Other devices can show it immediately. The final message keeps the same ID.

The attachment goes under files/year/month/message-ID/original-filename , so two messages can carry files of the same name. Once upload returns a DriveItem , replaceMessage() commits type: "file" to the original chunk with an ETag check. The ETag is the server’s version marker: the check makes sure nothing else has modified the target chunk in the meantime. Part two covers concurrent writes in detail.

Failure point What happens next
Placeholder registration Try to remove a possibly written placeholder and return upload-failed .
Attachment upload fails or is cancelled Try to remove the placeholder and retain failed local state for follow-up.
Upload succeeds but final commit fails Return reconciling , keep the attachment details and allow a commit retry.

files/retry-commit rebuilds the message from the existing attachment. If the final record already exists it returns it, without uploading again. These are separate writes; a later failure doesn’t roll back an earlier success. The intermediate state tells the client whether to retry the transfer or just the commit.

There’s a month-boundary edge case. Attachment paths use the request’s createdAt , but message writes obtain the target month with getUtcMonth() at call time. A long upload or retry across midnight at month end can separate the two. Version 1.0.3 doesn’t pin one immutable month context across the whole send.

# Upload sessions and chunks

Once you select a file, the UI hands the upload to the runtime on your device. The runtime handles authentication, transfers and storage. Extensions dispatch to the background runtime; the native iOS app uses its own entry point. Small files can be passed as Base64 and written to the target’s /content endpoint using HTTP PUT . Larger files stay as Blobs in shared IndexedDB. The runtime creates a Graph upload session with createUploadSession and sends successive slices to its dedicated URL, avoiding a large Base64 round trip.

# Selecting a transfer method and chunk size

On slower connections, each completed chunk lets the client update the progress bar with the number of bytes OneDrive has accepted. If a chunk fails, only that chunk needs to be retried. Regular chunk sizes use Graph’s 320 KB alignment; the final chunk carries the remainder.

OneDrop chooses 320 KB, 640 KB or 5 MB, respectively one, two or sixteen base units. Non-images larger than 4 MB use 5 MB chunks; other files of at least 1 MB use 640 KB; smaller files use 320 KB. Smaller chunks report progress sooner; larger ones reduce request count.

shouldUseUploadSession() starts using sessions at 320 KB. That threshold is OneDrop’s choice. MAX_DIRECT_FILE_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024 guards the direct upload function and helps select chunk size. Neither value is an overall attachment size limit.

# Validating and submitting chunks

Direct upload checks the decoded byte count against the file size; session upload checks the Blob size. For direct uploads, directory preparation and content transfer each have a twelve-second budget. Otherwise directory requests could use up nearly all the time before the upload even starts. User cancellation and timeout return distinct errors.

Creating the session requires a Graph token. After that the client sends slices directly to uploadUrl with Content-Range: bytes start-end/total . The end is inclusive, hence end - 1 in the code.

A partial upload normally returns 202 Accepted . A saved file returns 200 OK or 201 Created with the resulting DriveItem . The client validates its ID, name and size, constructs the attachment metadata and marks progress complete. If all local chunks have been sent but no completion response arrives, it reports an error. Sending the last byte alone doesn’t establish that Graph saved the file.

# Retrying and recovering progress

Each chunk gets up to three attempts with waits of 500 milliseconds and one second. Although the code lists 429 and several 5xx statuses, errors enter the same catch block and other non-cancellation exceptions can also retry. It doesn’t use Retry-After . Cancellation aborts the current request with AbortController .

A manual resend checks for an existing file at the original path with the same name and size. It can reuse that object, but doesn’t compare content hashes. Progress includes acknowledged bytes, the current chunk end and historical average speed. The UI uses that average to estimate progress. Failing to read or write local speed statistics doesn’t stop the transfer. The loop doesn’t persist the upload URL or offset or query the server for missing ranges after a restart, so closing the program can’t resume the session at its last chunk.

# Downloads and file reuse

# Download addresses and image previews

OneDrop looks up @microsoft.graph.downloadUrl by DriveItem ID, then delegates to the platform. The URL is temporary. The persistent message stores the ID.

For inline image previews it can also read /content , Base64-encode the bytes and embed them in a data URL for the UI. This preview path has a 4 MB limit, checked after reading the content. Ordinary uploads and downloads have separate rules.

# Reusing a download

The desktop extension maps cloud DriveItem IDs to browser download IDs. On reopening, it checks whether the download still exists, finished or was interrupted. It reuses a valid entry and discards a stale one before downloading again. Save As and forced downloads bypass reuse.

openExistingDownload() returns false for a missing record, removed file or interrupted download. An active transfer returns its status; a completed one records the new open operation.

# Confirming completion

browser.downloads.download() receives the URL, filename and options such as whether to show Save As. Its returned downloadId identifies a started browser task. It’s independent of the cloud driveItemId . The client removes control and path characters from filenames and handles name collisions.

It calls browser.downloads.search({ id: downloadId }) to check for in_progress , complete or interrupted . A completed file that still exists can be registered; interruption returns an error. For an active download it adds a browser.downloads.onChanged.addListener() callback, which receives the browser task ID and the properties that changed. OneDrop filters events by ID and queries the full task state again. It removes the listener once the outcome is known.

A download can finish between the first query and listener registration. If the new listener misses that notification, the UI can wait for a download that has already finished. An immediate second query closes that gap. In the code, finish() queries the state and handles the result:

Only a confirmed completion saves the mapping for reuse. An ordinary download interrupted with FILE_EXISTS gets up to three attempts to find an available name. Save As leaves the failure for the user to handle. A file already saved on the user’s device remains theirs when a cloud message is removed.

At this point messages and attachments are on OneDrive. Part two follows what happens when other devices read and modify them, and how archives and deleted records are maintained.

items.title: How OneDrop Adapts to Each Platform
items.content_html:
Part one and part two cover how OneDrop stores and syncs messages. This post looks at what the browser extension and native iOS app share, and where they need different implementations. I’m still referring to version 1.0.3.

# Sharing the message model

All the entry points work with the same message model. If each platform implemented merging, deletion tombstones and archiving separately, an edge case would need fixing in several places. Two devices could even interpret the same cloud data differently. OneDrop puts those rules in shared packages and lets each app assemble the pieces it needs.

Directory Responsibility
packages/core Message, month and settings types; runtime request protocol
packages/onedrive Graph requests, message chunks, archives, tombstones and attachments
packages/web-storage IndexedDB cache, pending sends and download records
packages/platform Platform bridge interfaces and runtime dependencies
packages/app-runtime Authorisation, device, settings and download services
packages/extension-runtime Dispatching background requests and handling extension entry points
packages/ui Shared React UI and interaction state
apps/edge , apps/ios Platform-specific assembly and native adapters

The core types don’t need to know about React components, browser download objects or Swift plugins. The UI sends a typed RuntimeRequest and receives a RuntimeResponse . In the extension the request travels over browser.runtime.sendMessage . A component can ask to send text, read a month or restore a message without assembling a Graph URL or an Authorization header.

# Platform capabilities

The same page behaves differently depending on its host. Desktop browsers have a download directory and a “Show in folder” command; mobile devices tend to use the system share sheet. Even browser extension entry points differ in which APIs they expose.

PlatformBridge connects UI requests such as “save this file” to the platform implementation. PlatformCapabilities declares the available operations:

Alongside request() , the bridge can look up and open downloads, prepare attachments, share files, and copy text or images. The UI offers actions according to those capabilities. On iOS Edge there’s no desktop download manager entry point, but system file sharing is available. The bridge retrieves the attachment, checks that the cached name, size and Blob agree, then prepares a shareable File .

Without a usable cache entry, the bridge reads the response stream and accumulates the number of bytes received so the UI can display progress. It gets the total from Content-Length when available and otherwise uses the attachment size in the message. Once the stream ends, it checks the Blob size, caches the attachment in IndexedDB and constructs the File . It also checks navigator.canShare before invoking system sharing. Preparing the file and opening the share sheet are separate steps.

That’s why the same attachment button can have a different final action. The message and DriveItem mean the same thing across platforms; the way the system receives the file differs. I don’t need to emulate a desktop API on every platform just to make the button look the same.

# Browser extension entry points

The extension uses WXT for development and builds, React for the UI, TypeScript for application logic and Manifest V3 for the extension. Desktop, Android and iOS share the extension code. Desktop opens a side panel, Android opens a separate mobile page and iOS uses an entry point suited to its extension environment. The app layer selects the entry point and bridge, so the shared UI doesn’t need a separate copy of every page.

There’s also a compatibility path for iOS Edge. Even if the browser opens the statically declared side-panel page, the app detects the platform and loads the iOS UI and bridge. The runtime and bridge handle differences such as the missing Identity API during login and the need to share downloads through the system. Shipping one extension package doesn’t make mobile APIs behave like their desktop counterparts.

# Native iOS

The native app uses Capacitor to host the shared React UI in a WebView, a browser view embedded in the app. Native plugins provide access to system features. For login, the OneDropAuth Swift plugin opens the authorisation flow with ASWebAuthenticationSession and stores and retrieves tokens through Keychain. The browser extension described in part one uses browser.storage.local ; on native iOS both the authorisation window and credential storage belong to the plugin.

The shared OneDrive code needs an access token, local state and a way to send events. The app supplies those functions at startup. That’s what dependency injection means here: the business logic calls the supplied functions without repeatedly checking which platform it’s on. The iOS entry point wires up native implementations and forwards message requests to the same shared functions. The native download plugin saves, locates and opens files while the UI continues to work with the same attachment metadata.

Device settings follow the same division. Each installation generates an anonymous UUID and stores its platform, display name and preferences in settings/devices/<device-id>.json . Removing a device from the list removes its settings document. Messages and attachments from that device have a separate lifecycle, described in part two’s deletion and cleanup flow.

For me, OneDrop is still a little tool for passing things between my devices. Once OneDrive took over storage, the recurring questions were about state: when a send counts as complete, what another device sees, what can resume after a failure and what survives deletion. Keeping those rules shared and leaving login, downloads and entry points to each platform gives me a clear place to make the next change.

items.title: OneDrop Storage and Multi-Device Sync (Part Two)
items.content_html:
Part one covered authorisation, the storage layout and file transfers. What happens after a message has been saved? This part follows it through concurrent edits, history, deletion and recovery. The implementation described here is still OneDrop 1.0.3.

# Synchronisation, conflicts and archives

# Reading messages and using the cache

# When a client syncs

Clients pull changes when the interface opens, comes to the foreground, refreshes manually or needs to read data as part of sending. There’s no server of mine continually pushing updates. Once the browser closes, you can’t treat it as an always-online messenger.

On returning to the foreground, the UI checks the time since the previous sync. This avoids rereading the month every time you switch windows. Normal mode checks after 30 seconds, Reduced mode after five minutes. Manual mode doesn’t trigger a sync from this foreground check.

# Reading a month and reusing cached chunks

The client lists files under messages/YYYY-MM , requests 200 items per page, follows @odata.nextLink and reads the chunks in numerical order. The 200-item limit applies to a single listing request. It doesn’t limit the number of messages or chunks in the month. A missing monthly directory is a valid empty state; a failed request is an error. Pagination URLs are checked against the expected Graph API scope.

The cache stores more than the merged list. For each chunk it retains the DriveItem ID, ETag, parsed document and message line numbers. An ETag identifies the version returned by the server. If the version matches and line information is present, the cached document can be reused. Changed chunks are downloaded and parsed, up to three at once. A growing history doesn’t mean downloading every JSON body on every refresh. In the code below, a matching version and complete line information let OneDrop reuse the local record. Otherwise it calls downloadDocument() .

After parsing, OneDrop merges by ID, sorts by createdAt and ID, and applies deletion markers from tombstones . Identical records with the same ID collapse to one. Different contents for a single ID produce a conflict record with source files and line numbers so the choice can be resolved later.

# Following an upload in progress

Part one introduced the file-uploading placeholder. Other devices can see it before the attachment finishes. To pick up the final file message promptly, the visible, signed-in UI polls after waits of 2, 5, 8 and 10 seconds, then continues at 10-second intervals. Once the accumulated waits reach 120 seconds it ends the round and marks outstanding placeholders unresponsive. That total counts time spent waiting between requests, excluding the requests themselves.

If the attachment is already stored and the local record is committing , the client retries the final message on the same schedule, stopping at the round limit. An online event attempts those commits again and cleans up placeholders left by failed uploads. This work resumes from local state when the client is running or connectivity returns.

# Loading earlier messages

Scrolling back expands more batches within the loaded months and fetches one earlier UTC month. Each read carries a request version and a local write version; the client checks both before applying the response so a stale read can’t overwrite a newer local action. It also remembers a visible message as a scroll anchor. When older items arrive above it, the message you were reading stays in view.

# ETags and concurrent writes

Reads can merge several chunks, but a write has to protect each chunk against concurrent changes. Suppose A and B both read version v1 . A adds a message and writes successfully. If B now writes back a full JSON document built from its old copy, it can erase A’s message.

# Check the version and retry

When updating an existing chunk, OneDrop sends the ETag it read in If-Match . The server accepts the write only if the version still matches. After A’s update, B’s condition no longer holds.

A changed file can produce 412 Precondition Failed ; competing object creation can produce 409 Conflict . For these responses OneDrop invalidates the cache and retries from the cloud:

The next iteration reads a fresh snapshot, merges by message ID and decides where to write. If the ID is already present it returns the existing result, avoiding a duplicate append on a retried send. After five unsuccessful rounds it reports the conflict so the caller can retain the failure state.

A new chunk has no previous ETag, so OneDrop asks Graph to fail if the name already exists. If two devices both try to create 0002.json , one succeeds. The other rereads the month before deciding where to write.

If a directory has been deleted and Graph returns 404, OneDrop clears the corresponding cache and tries to locate the directory again.

# Network failures and local write ordering

A network error has different semantics. The server may have committed the request even if the client never received its response. The write function invalidates the cache and reports the error without automatically replaying the write. A subsequent sync or explicit retry can inspect the message ID to determine what happened.

Within one runtime, a Promise queue serialises modifications to monthly messages. Operations across devices still depend on server-side conditional writes. Keeping the queue at the message-write layer also means a large attachment needn’t block text messages for the entire duration of its upload.

# Chunking and damaged records

# Choosing a chunk

A single ever-growing monthly JSON file would make every append more expensive. OneDrop tries the last active chunk first. If the proposed append exceeds the 256 KiB soft limit, it starts a new chunk. The final document has a separate 320 KB hard limit, and chunk numbers stop at 9999. Exceeding those limits is an error; reaching the numbering limit seems unlikely for message metadata alone.

The soft limit decides when to roll over. The hard limit applies to every final chunk, including a new one or an existing one after a placeholder is replaced. Older chunks remain readable. Committing a file message requires finding the chunk that contains its placeholder, regardless of which chunk is now last.

The code first merges the message into the last chunk to measure the result. If it exceeds the soft limit, OneDrop starts a new chunk and checks its size against the hard limit before writing.

# Corruption and conflicting contents

A read can collect malformed JSON and conflicting records while still displaying the readable remainder. A strict read aborts. Treating invalid JSON as an empty list would lose the distinction between damaged and genuinely empty data.

An ordinary append can proceed while leaving a damaged file untouched. The next chunk number accounts for damaged chunks so their paths won’t be reused. After rereading the remote month, a known conflict for the target message ID blocks the write. The cached fast path means there isn’t a complete remote conflict scan before every write. Archiving is stricter: any damaged source file or conflicting message blocks consolidation.

When two versions have the same ID, silently keeping the last one read could discard the other version. Instead, the user chooses which source to retain. resolveMessageConflict() removes the record from the other source chunks with ETag checks. If another device edits a source in the meantime, the user must recheck it before the earlier decision can be applied.

# Archiving history

# Building and verifying the archive

Once a UTC month has been over for more than 24 hours, OneDrop can consolidate it into archive/YYYY-MM.json . The delay gives end-of-month writes some breathing room. Subsequent history reads can then fetch fewer files. Eligible history reads try the archive first. If there is no archive, the read fails, or it takes more than eight seconds, they fall back to the source chunks. Current tombstones apply to archive reads too.

Creation uses conflictBehavior=fail so an existing archive won’t be overwritten. After writing, OneDrop reads it back and compares the serialised result with the intended document. If an archive already exists, its contents must match the visible source month. Damaged files, unresolved messages or an inconsistent existing archive leave the task blocked.

# Retries and timeout reporting

Task state is persisted locally. cooling-down waits for the next retry, auth-paused waits for authorisation, blocked needs a data problem resolved, and succeeded records success. Ordinary retries wait five minutes, thirty minutes, six hours and then twenty-four hours. Reopening the interface doesn’t immediately repeat a task known to be failing.

After thirty seconds the task can report a timeout. That notification doesn’t cancel the underlying operation. The client still waits for its actual outcome, so a later success can update the task state.

# Source cleanup and recovery limits

A successful archive leaves the monthly source directory in place initially. The task saves a digest of the archive and sets cleanupPending . Cleanup rereads the raw archive and checks that digest before trying to remove the source directory. A failed cleanup can be retried independently.

The check returns early if the archive is missing, there’s no saved digest, or the digest no longer matches.

There is a limitation here: the digest verifies the archive, but the implementation doesn’t check that the source still matches its archived version immediately before deletion. Another device could have changed the source since the archive was created.

The archive also contains visible messages after tombstone filtering. It doesn’t preserve every original deleted record. Cleaning the source directory can therefore remove the only remaining recovery source for a deleted message. Recovery has to check what still exists.

# Deletion, recovery and physical cleanup

# Tombstones and retention

Removing a message from a local array would let the next sync bring it back. Removing it from one chunk still leaves the possibility of a stale writer. OneDrop records deletion separately as a tombstone , and all read paths apply the same deletion state.

A tombstone records messageId , originalMonth , deletedAt and optionally recovery . It’s saved by original month in tombstones/YYYY-MM.json . Monthly and archive reads filter the matching IDs. Hiding a message therefore doesn’t require its attachment and original JSON to disappear at the same instant. The monthly read below fetches the set of deleted IDs and excludes them from the merged result. It leaves the source files in place.

Updating and removing tombstones also use read, merge and conditional write, with up to five attempts on conflict. Otherwise deleting one message on A could overwrite a deletion marker B had just added for a different message.

The deletion action records its recovery policy: disabled, 3, 7, 10 or 30 days, or forever. Finite retention can include an explicit recoverableUntil . For older records without the information, cleanup falls back to ten days after deletion. Disabling recovery makes the record eligible immediately; remote objects still go through the cleanup process.

# The recycle bin and restoring messages

A tombstone stores deletion state, not a full copy of the text or attachment. For the recycle bin, OneDrop reads the raw archive and unfiltered records in the source chunks, merges them and looks for the matching ID. A hidden message can appear there while its original content remains available.

Identical records can merge. Contradictory versions with the same ID don’t count as one unambiguously recoverable message. If the source is gone, the client doesn’t construct a placeholder from the tombstone and present it as recoverable.

Restore checks the tombstone and original again, removes the marker, then clears the monthly cache. If either the tombstone or the original is missing, the restore function returns an error here. Otherwise, the next normal read includes the message. There’s no new message ID or attachment upload.

Retention defines cleanup eligibility; it isn’t an independent backup. A manually removed original or a source lost during archive cleanup can’t be reconstructed from an ID. Even an intact file message doesn’t guarantee the attachment is still there: external operations can move or delete it.

# Cleaning up expired data

# Selecting eligible items

A separate cleanup process removes remote attachments and metadata. Automatic scans run at 24-hour intervals and inspect up to twenty eligible items per round. A manual cleanup skips the normal interval, expiry wait and ordinary round limit. Automatic scans skip permanent retention; disabled recovery is eligible from deletion time. The code below calculates the earliest cleanup time as eligibleAt . Automatic scans skip records that haven’t reached it, while manual cleanup skips that time check.

Before deleting anything, the client reads the source and checks the month implied by the message timestamp. If it can’t identify the record uniquely, it stops processing that item. An absent record alongside a damaged file warrants investigation: an empty set of successfully parsed records doesn’t prove cleanup is complete.

# Checking references and deleting in order

For a file message, the client checks whether another undeleted message in the currently read month refers to the same driveItemId . If it does, it keeps the attachment. Otherwise it locates files/year/month/message-ID , verifies that it’s a folder containing the target DriveItem , and only then deletes that attachment folder. This check doesn’t build a global reference index over all of OneDrive.

After handling the attachment it removes metadata from message chunks or the archive. JSON rewrites use ETags. A change or conflict defers the operation and leaves the tombstone for later. The marker is removed last, once the metadata step is confirmed, and the item is marked complete.

An intermediate state is possible: the attachment is gone but a conditional metadata update hasn’t succeeded yet. A local maintenance queue serialises restore and cleanup on one device; it doesn’t lock every device. A subsequent restore must still recheck its sources.

Two other cases are worth distinguishing.

  • A failed local send that never reached the cloud can be removed from IndexedDB after confirmation, without creating a cloud tombstone .
  • A file the user has already downloaded to a system directory is their own copy. Cleaning up its message or deleting its download registration doesn’t delete that local file.

items.title: OneDrop: Sending Text and Files through OneDrive
items.content_html:
OneDrop is a tool I built so you can send text and files between your devices through your own OneDrive. This post covers why I made it, where it’s available and what I’d like to improve. I left the implementation details for a separate post. I’ve since written them up in part one and part two of my series on storage and sync.

# Why I made OneDrop

I use Edge on pretty much everything. It came with Windows and I got used to it, so even on my Mac and phone I install it and make it my default browser.

Edge’s built-in Drop used to be how I moved things between devices. I used it all the time. When a later version of Edge removed the feature, I wanted to keep that habit going.

I could send files to myself in WeChat, and there’s no shortage of file transfer tools. But most of the time I’m just passing a link, a bit of text or an attachment to another device. Opening a separate app always felt like one step too many. Edge is usually open already. I wanted to be able to send the item right there and get on with what I was doing.

# Why OneDrive

I didn’t want to run a server just to move things between my own devices. The cost and maintenance didn’t make sense for this use.

Since I was building for Edge, using a Microsoft account and OneDrive felt natural. Many Edge users already have an account. You sign in with your own account and the text and files stay in your own OneDrive. There’s no separate storage service for me to maintain.

A Microsoft account includes 5 GB of free cloud storage, shared with other content on the account. That’s normally enough for my snippets and occasional files. If your OneDrive is already pretty full, check the space available first.

# What it’s like to use

Text and file transfers share a single message list. On desktop Edge the extension opens in the sidebar, so I can use it without leaving the page.

That’s the experience I wanted to keep: send something here when I need it on another device, then pick it up there.

You can go back through your message history. I wanted long-term archiving too, so OneDrop could match Drop’s features as closely as possible.

The free 5 GB can fill up. OneDrop lets you delete individual messages and has a recycle bin, so you can keep the records you want and remove the rest. Deleting a message from the list removes its record there. To finish deleting it and reclaim the storage, clear it from the recycle bin too.

# Where it’s available

The desktop extension is available from the Edge Add-ons store.

Mobile installation takes more work. Edge has a submission process for mobile extensions. I submitted the Android and iOS forms, but at the time of writing I hadn’t received a reply to either. The desktop store installation route doesn’t work for them yet.

For early access, the GitHub release includes a CRX package. It requires developer mode and the corresponding test browser: Edge Canary on Android or the TestFlight version of Edge on iOS. The installation guide lists the steps. They don’t carry over directly to stable mobile Edge.

On iOS there’s also an IPA for the native application. It’s intended for import into LiveContainer, which you need to set up first. It isn’t an App Store build or something you can install by tapping the download.

# Rough edges and plans

The hurdle I notice most is still installation on mobile. The desktop version has a store listing, while both a test browser and LiveContainer need extra setup. That’s an awkward first impression for a tool I made to save myself a few steps.

I’ll keep an eye on the mobile extension submissions. I’ve also considered a standalone Android app, but I haven’t set a date. For now I want to get the everyday operations right: sending, viewing and clearing items across devices.

The source is on GitHub. If you have similar habits, the installation requirements are a good place to start. At the time of this post, the project had reached 1.0.3. Most features were in place and had been through an initial round of testing. If you run into anything, leave a comment or open a GitHub issue.

items.title: Managing Projects with Git and GitHub
items.content_html:
Git records versions. GitHub hosts repositories and provides a place to discuss issues and review code. Knowing how to use both is a basic development skill. Pushing code is only one step. A typical change also raises questions about branches, commits, review, automated checks and release. This post follows one change through that process.

# Organising a repository

# What belongs in the README?

When you open a project for the first time, you want to know what it does, what’s working so far, and how to run it. A README should answer those questions up front, then point you to the docs for more detail.

A useful order is introduction, demo, main features, installation or startup, contributing and licence. For a graphical application, one real screenshot often conveys more than a long feature list. Include the prerequisites and commands someone needs to install dependencies and run it.

In my DungeonTavern README, I start with the project and documentation links, show the actual scene, then cover features and startup. Long design notes can live in separate documents. Relative links to files and screenshots continue to work when readers switch branches or download the source.

# Explain usage and contributions

The licence describes permitted uses. A CONTRIBUTING.md can explain environment setup, validation and contribution submission. Link both from the README. Templates make these reports more consistent. An issue template can ask for reproduction steps. A pull request template can ask what changed and how the contributor checked it.

# Exclude files that don’t belong in history

Use .gitignore to exclude files you don’t want under version control. A Node.js project might ignore installed dependencies, build products and local configuration:

Keep only variable names and dummy values in .env.example . Whether to track dist/ depends on distribution: some repositories intentionally version their built output.

Adding an already tracked file to .gitignore won’t untrack it. To remove it from the index and keep the local copy:

Old commits still contain it. Revoke or rotate a secret that was committed.

# Create a branch for the change

Check for unfinished local changes first, then create the working branch from an up-to-date main branch. The example assumes a main branch named main and a remote named origin :

--ff-only stops if local and remote histories have diverged. That gives you a chance to inspect both sides. Use a name that describes the change, such as fix/category-wrap or feat/search . Keep a release script edit separate from a category layout fix so each can be reviewed, reverted and located in history independently. Short-lived branches suit many small projects; version branches become useful when maintaining multiple release lines.

# Bring in changes from main

Commit your work in progress or stash it. Once the working tree and index are clean, fetch:

Choose one of these approaches according to the project’s conventions:

A merge preserves the existing commits and can join diverged histories with a merge commit. A rebase replays changes on a new base and gives the replayed commits new IDs.

Situation Approach Reason
Others share the branch or work on top of it Prefer a merge Their existing commit IDs remain valid.
The work is entirely local A rebase is reasonable Nobody else depends on the old IDs.
The branch was pushed but only you use it Follow the repository convention Updating the remote after a rebase usually requires a force push. Check who depends on it first.
The target requires linear history Use a compatible rebase, squash or fast-forward A merge commit would violate the rule; a fast-forward creates none.

Coordinate before rewriting shared history. Don’t rewrite a public main branch simply to sync your work. Choosing a PR merge method below concerns a later step.

Resolve conflicts in the files, then mark them resolved with git add . Complete the merge commit or run git rebase --continue as appropriate. To abandon the operation, use git merge --abort or git rebase --abort . Restore stashed changes with git stash pop ; restoring can itself cause conflicts. Run the relevant checks even after a clean textual merge.

# Organise changes into commits

Inspect the changes before committing:

git diff shows unstaged changes and git diff --cached shows what the next commit will contain. Stage selected hunks with git add -p ; add new files separately after checking status.

Implementation, tests and documentation can belong in one commit when they accomplish one thing. Splitting mechanically by file makes less sense than separating unrelated formatting, debugging files and behaviour changes. Mixing those together makes reverting the functional change much harder.

For a public project, English commit messages can help contributors who speak other languages. Follow existing language conventions. Git itself doesn’t require English. Describe the effect of the change, with context where needed:

Once you’ve checked the staged changes, run git commit and enter the message in your editor. A subject like the one above tells you what changed when you browse the history. An entry like update or fix bug leaves you guessing. The Git project’s contribution guidelines also ask contributors to group changes logically and explain why they made them.

Prefixes such as feat: and fix: are a team convention and can help generate release notes. Use them if they suit the project. What matters is that the messages are clear and consistent within the repository.

If you’ve just committed and discover a related change you left out, stage it and run the following while the commit is still unshared:

Amending changes the commit ID. If others already depend on it, adding a follow-up commit is usually easier than rewriting history just to tidy up the message.

# Open and merge a pull request

Push the working branch and establish its upstream:

Open a PR against the intended base. Explain the problem, the change and how you verified it. Here’s an example description:

Only list checks actually performed. Verify that Closes #42 points to the issue this change resolves. Use a draft PR to discuss an unfinished approach. Review existing behaviour and edge cases as well as the new code. Push follow-up fixes to the same branch; the PR updates automatically. The VS Code contribution guide asks contributors to keep PRs focused and avoid unrelated formatting, which makes changes easier to review.

# Choose a merge method

Syncing the working branch during development and deciding what history lands on main are distinct decisions. A branch rebased locally can still be squash-merged. A branch kept current with merge commits can also be squashed.

GitHub option Result on the target When it fits
Create a merge commit Keeps the branch commits and adds a merge commit The full branch relationship is worth retaining.
Squash and merge Records the PR as one new commit Many small fixes together form a single change.
Rebase and merge Replays the commits individually, with new IDs and no merge commit The separate commits already tell the intended story.

Follow the project’s convention.

# Clean up after the merge

After confirming the merge, remove the remote working branch if appropriate and update local main. A squash of commits A, B and C produces a new S on main. A merge commit keeps A, B and C and joins them with M.

git branch -d checks ancestry against the tracked upstream, or against the current branch if there’s no upstream. It doesn’t compare resulting content. A squash-merged branch can therefore report not fully merged . Confirm the PR landed and that the working branch has no later unmerged commits. Only then, if needed:

Capital -D skips the ancestry check. Removing the local branch reference doesn’t undo the squash commit.

# Automating checks and releases with GitHub Actions

Running a PR’s build and tests automatically gives reviewers a result and a log for every update.

# CI/CD

Continuous integration means integrating code frequently and running automated builds and tests to catch problems early. For example, a project can build and run its tests on each PR. Continuous delivery also prepares a releasable package, with release potentially left to a person. Continuous deployment sends passing changes to production without that final approval.

These are workflows made up of concrete operations such as testing, building, uploading and deploying. GitHub Actions can orchestrate them, and can also perform unrelated repository tasks such as applying labels.

# Add a check workflow

Store workflows under .github/workflows/ . Events such as pushes, PR changes and manual dispatch trigger workflows. Each workflow contains one or more jobs. Each job runs on a runner, and its steps run commands or invoke actions in order. Use needs to express dependencies between jobs.

For this example the project uses Node.js 24, has a committed package-lock.json , and defines CI-compatible test and build scripts in package.json . Create .github/workflows/ci.yml :

This workflow only checks the application. It runs on PR updates and checks main after a merge. For manual dispatch the workflow must already exist on the default branch. npm ci installs from the lockfile. If there’s no test script, substitute the project’s actual check command. When strict action pinning is required, use a verified full commit SHA.

In Actions, open a run and find the first failing step. Its context distinguishes dependency installation, test and build failures. This actual OneDrop CI run includes formatting, TypeScript compilation, tests and two build targets:

# Caches, artifacts and releases

cache: npm reuses npm’s package cache, not node_modules ; the workflow still runs npm ci . Artifacts preserve results such as installers or test reports for later jobs or downloads.

A separate release workflow might trigger from a tag, a published release or manual dispatch. Deployment environment protections can require approval where the repository and plan support them. The check example needs only contents: read . Grant additional permissions only to jobs that need them. Put tokens in Secrets. External fork PRs have restrictions on tokens and secrets: avoid executing untrusted PR code in a privileged pull_request_target context.

# Protect main

GitHub offers classic branch protections and rulesets. Multiple rulesets can apply alongside existing protections. The table uses the English labels from Rulesets. The classic branch protection page groups and names its options slightly differently.

Rule Purpose
Require a pull request before merging Route changes through a PR.
Require status checks to pass Require named checks such as CI.
Required approvals Set the approval count within the PR rule.
Block force pushes Protect existing history.
Restrict deletions Protect the branch from deletion.

Require linear history rules out merge commits on the target. Select compatible squash or rebase merges. See GitHub’s ruleset reference.

Run a workflow at least once before selecting its check name. Path filters or conditional jobs can otherwise leave a PR waiting for a check that never appears. For a solo project, avoid requiring approvals nobody can give; larger projects can add reviewers or code owners. Also check plan availability and who can bypass a rule.

# Contributing through a fork

With write access, push a working branch to the project. Otherwise fork the project on GitHub, clone your fork locally and propose changes upstream. Forking creates a hosting relationship; cloning downloads a repository.

After cloning your fork, origin generally points to it. Add a remote for the original project, commonly called upstream . These names are conventions. Replace OWNER and REPOSITORY with the original project’s owner and name. If upstream already exists, verify its URL instead of adding it again.

Here main follows upstream and personal changes stay on working branches. Handle uncommitted work first, then sync:

Both fast-forward checks can stop on divergence between local main, your fork and the original repository. Inspect the unique commits and decide what to keep before merging or rebasing. A force push would rewrite history without answering that question.

Create a working branch, make the change, push to your fork’s origin and open the PR against the branch requested by the project.

Read the contribution guide for the target branch, tests and whether an issue discussion is expected first.

# Managing large files with Git LFS

Images, models and audio sources may need versioning alongside code. Git LFS stores small pointers in Git and keeps the contents in LFS storage. GitHub rejects ordinary Git files over 100 MiB. Consider LFS for required versioned binaries, ignore build caches and put downloadable release installers in Releases.

Once you’ve installed Git LFS, initialise it in the repository and add a tracking rule. Here’s an example for PSD files that ordinary Git hasn’t tracked yet:

git lfs track writes the rule to .gitattributes . Commit that file so collaborators use the same rules. Check git lfs ls-files to confirm the files are managed by LFS. Collaborators need Git LFS too. If a checkout contains only pointer text, run git lfs pull .

Adding a tracking rule doesn’t shrink existing history. Migrating old binaries rewrites commits: back up, define the scope and coordinate with collaborators before doing so. Check the account’s storage and download allowances as well.

# Tagging a version

After confirming the exact release commit, create and push an annotated tag:

A GitHub Release builds on a tag with release notes and downloadable assets. Document visible changes, fixes and upgrade requirements. Attach built installers separately; an automatically generated source archive isn’t the compiled application.

# Undoing changes

Run git status and git diff first to see which changes you want to keep.

Situation Command Effect
Reselect staged changes git restore --staged path/to/file Keeps working-tree edits.
Discard unwanted unstaged changes to a tracked file git restore path/to/file Restores the index version and discards those edits.
Reorganise the most recent unshared commit git reset --soft HEAD~1 Removes the commit from the branch tip while retaining staged changes.
Undo an ordinary commit on a shared branch git revert COMMIT Adds an inverse commit and preserves history.

The default mixed reset also resets the index but keeps working-tree changes. A hard reset overwrites affected working-tree changes too. Reverts can conflict; reverting a merge requires deciding which parent is the mainline. Fixes and reversions on public branches can go through the same branch, PR and check process.

items.title: Customising My Zsh Prompt
items.content_html:
Oh My Zsh manages Zsh configuration and comes with themes, plugins and some handy defaults. I originally picked Zsh and Oh My Zsh because I wanted a better-looking terminal. I tried a lot of the bundled themes. Most were too busy for my taste, and the simpler ones weren’t quite what I wanted either. Eventually I wrote my own.

Here’s the theme I use, how the prompt works and which plugins I’ve kept.

# My current prompt

The theme itself is six lines:

The first line shows the final directory component. The second adds the Git information and status symbol. The last four set the Git prefix, suffix, and indicators for clean and modified working trees. I deliberately gave DIRTY and CLEAN the same value. The base theme shows the branch without distinguishing local changes.

# Installing a custom theme

Oh My Zsh’s customisation conventions support themes under $ZSH_CUSTOM/themes . With the default installation, that’s ~/.oh-my-zsh/custom/themes . Keeping a separate .zsh-theme file makes it easy to find and edit later.

Create the directory, respecting a custom value of ZSH_CUSTOM if you have one:

Save the six lines as sycamore-simple.zsh-theme , then edit the existing ZSH_THEME setting in ~/.zshrc . Omit the filename extension:

Put it before source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh so it’s in place at initialisation. Open a new terminal to check the result.

# Understanding the configuration

If you’d rather start with a few examples, skip to common variations and come back when you want to change a particular detail.

# What controls the prompt?

Oh My Zsh uses ZSH_THEME to find the file and supplies helpers such as git_prompt_info . Zsh variables and prompt expansion determine what gets drawn.

Variable When it appears
PROMPT / PS1 Main prompt waiting for input. Both names refer to the same parameter.
RPROMPT / RPS1 Right-hand prompt while editing a command.
PS2 / PROMPT2 Continuation prompt for unfinished input, such as a quote or loop.
RPS2 Right-hand continuation prompt.
PS3 Selection prompt in a select loop.
PS4 Prefix on execution trace lines.

Most themes concentrate on the first two. Here are examples for continuation, selection and debugging:

In PS2, %_ names the unfinished shell construct; if you see this prompt after Return, the command needs more input. PS3 affects select menus. In PS4, %N and %i show the script or function name and line number. Use set -x to start tracing and set +x when finished.

# Prompt expansion reference

Zsh expands percent sequences when displaying the prompt. This is a selection from the prompt expansion manual.

Purpose Sequences Display
Directory %c Last component, with home abbreviation
Directory %~ Full path with home or named-directory substitutions
Directory %/ , %d Full path without home abbreviation
Identity %n , %m , %M Username, short hostname, full hostname
Terminal %l , %y Terminal name with different prefix handling
Status %? , %j , %L Exit status, job count, shell nesting level
Privilege %# Hash for a privileged shell, percent otherwise
History %h , %! History event number
Time %T , %* 24-hour time without or with seconds
Date %D{%Y-%m-%d} Formatted date
Colour %F{cyan} / %f , %K{black} / %k Set/reset foreground and background
Style %B / %b , %U / %u , %S / %s Start/end bold, underline or standout
Literals %% , %) Percent sign or closing parenthesis

A number before a directory escape limits the component count: %2~ keeps the last two, useful if you want the project name without filling the line. The PS2 and PS4 examples above show how to use %_ , %N and %i . Related debugging escapes include %^ for unfinished constructs in reverse order, %x and %I for the defining file and line, and %e for evaluation depth.

For a two-line prompt put a literal newline in the string or concatenate $'\n' . In ordinary single quotes, backslash-n remains two characters.

Format Meaning
%t , %@ 12-hour time with am/pm
%D , %w , %W Two-digit year-month-day, abbreviated weekday and day, or month/day/two-digit year
%D{format} A strftime-style format, e.g. %Y , %m , %d , %H:%M:%S

The codes inside date braces have their own meanings. Zsh adds unpadded day ( %f ), 24-hour ( %K ) and 12-hour ( %L ) fields. Fractional seconds use %. ; %6. requests six digits, %9. or %N nine. Actual precision depends on the clock. Forms such as %-d suppress padding. Other extensions depend on the system.

  • %E clears from the cursor to the end of the line.
  • %{...%} encloses nonprinting sequences such as colour codes so they don’t count towards prompt width. Keep ordinary text outside this wrapper.
  • Inside such a sequence, %G accounts for one visible character cell and %2G for two.

The older %c and %. show the final directory component, and %C does the same without abbreviating home as ~ . The manual deprecates the older directory forms %c and %. in favour of %1~ , and %C in favour of %1/ . I kept %c above to show my actual theme.

A function can compute values first and leave formatting to the prompt using the psvar array. %v selects the first item, %2v the second; negative indices count from the end. With psvar=(demo) , %v displays demo.

# Conditional output

The second line of my theme uses %(?:success:failure) to change the final symbol between green and red according to the previous exit status. Add %? to display the numeric status itself.

The question mark selects the test. The two colons separate test, true branch and false branch. Both can instead be dots, as in %(?.success.failure) . In the general form %(test.true.false) , the comparison value nnn can appear before or after the opening parenthesis; it defaults to zero.

Test True when
! The shell has privileges.
# , g Effective user or group ID equals n.
? Previous exit status equals n.
_ At least n shell constructs are open.
/ , C The absolute path has at least n components; root counts as zero.
c , . , ~ The substituted path has at least n components.
D , d , w Month, day of month or weekday equals n. Months are zero-based; Sunday is zero.
T , t Hour or minute equals n.
e , j , L Evaluation depth, jobs or shell level is at least n.
S SECONDS is at least n; this is not the previous command’s duration.
v , V psvar has at least n entries, or its nth entry is set and nonempty.
l At least n characters have been printed on the line; a negative argument tests space left to the opposite edge.

For example, %(!.#.>) displays a hash for a privileged shell and a greater-than sign otherwise. Choose another delimiter if your branch text contains a dot. Use %) for a literal closing parenthesis in a branch. Conditionals can nest. Negative condition arguments use their absolute value except for the remaining-width form of l .

# Dynamic information

The Git branch changes while the shell stays open. I put $(git_prompt_info) inside the prompt so command substitution runs the helper each time the prompt is displayed. This requires:

Oh My Zsh already enables this option. For a standalone test you’ll need to enable it; the colour variables and Git helper still come from Oh My Zsh. Quoting controls when substitution happens:

Single quotes keep the call for the next prompt expansion. Double quotes evaluate it when assigning the variable. I used single quotes for the Git helper and the battery and Python examples below.

# Common variations

Each example starts with my six-line theme and changes one thing so you can compare the results.

# Show the full path

Replace the first line of the theme with the following to show the full path:

To show your home directory as ~ , replace %/ with %~ . Both keep the full directory hierarchy.

# Show the username

To show the username and hostname before the path, append this line to the theme:

If you only want the username, replace %n@%m with %n .

# Put the time on the right

Append the time to the left prompt after loading the theme:

Or keep the space between directory and input free by setting the right prompt:

Choose one. The battery and Python examples also assign RPROMPT; assigning it again replaces the previous value. The time is evaluated when the prompt is displayed. It isn’t a continuously ticking clock, and the right prompt gives up space as the command line grows.

# Show the battery level

Here’s the macOS example. Put the function and right prompt after the theme:

Without battery information it displays nothing. The %% in the function’s output becomes one percent sign during prompt expansion. The query runs on prompt refresh, without a background polling task.

# Show the Python project, environment and version

If you switch between Python projects and environments often, you can show the project marker, environment name and interpreter version in the prompt. Place this function and right prompt after the six theme lines:

It checks the current directory for pyproject.toml or requirements.txt , reads the environment from VIRTUAL_ENV or CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV , and reports the version of python3 on PATH. It doesn’t search parent directories or read version-manager configuration. If prompt refreshes are frequent, cache the version after changing environments instead of launching an interpreter every time.

# Mark a dirty Git working tree

I gave clean and dirty trees the same suffix in the original. Change DIRTY to add an asterisk when the tree has changes:

Oh My Zsh handles status detection; its settings affect whether untracked files count. Run git status to see the actual changes.

# Plugins

These are the six plugins enabled in my setup:

Put this in .zshrc before Oh My Zsh initialises. The theme defines the prompt; plugins add commands and input behaviour. Install a plugin before adding its name.

# git

Adds shortcuts such as gst for git status and gco for git checkout . The theme’s git_prompt_info helper comes with Oh My Zsh independently of this plugin.

# zsh-autosuggestions

Shows suggestions after the cursor, using command history by default. After running python test.py , typing the beginning can suggest the rest.

The upper line has suggestions turned off. In the lower line, grey text is the suggested part awaiting acceptance.

# zsh-syntax-highlighting

Colours the input so commands, arguments, quoted strings and some invalid input are easier to distinguish. The input highlighting is separate from the directory colour in the prompt.

# z

Jumps to previously visited directories. Once you’ve visited a project folder, z followed by part of its name can find it.

# extract

extract filename chooses the decompression tool for the archive type. I like having one command for the lot.

# web-search

Commands such as google zsh prompt open a query in the browser, handy when looking something up from the command line.

# Fonts and rendering

My default iTerm profile uses JetBrainsMonoNFM-Regular at 12 points. Select a font with the appropriate glyphs in your own terminal. If the  icon appears as a box, switch fonts or simply replace it with > in the theme.

Width matters too. My theme declares %1{%} as one cell. If the terminal draws it two cells wide, the cursor can end up in the wrong place.

items.title: Blog Themes I’ve Tried
items.content_html:
A few thoughts on blog themes I’ve used, or at least installed. I’ve also included two at the end that caught my eye while reading the documentation.

# What I like

I have a weakness for all the bells and whistles: falling cherry blossoms, a little Live2D character in the corner, effects when you click the mouse, a big beautiful cover image…

I’ve browsed and installed plenty of clean, elegant themes. They look good at first. Two days later I usually find myself changing themes again.

Maybe they just feel a little too blank for me.

# WordPress

WordPress has enough themes and plugins that whenever I felt like tinkering, there was always something else to install. I did run into a sluggish dashboard and slow-loading pages, though.

These are impressions from my own setup at the time. A slow site isn’t necessarily the theme’s fault. I quite liked Argon, for instance.

# Sakura

Sakura, maintained by mashirozx, is right up my street, down to the little details.

I followed quite a few tutorials to get different effects working. My Live2D character never made it past the default model; designing and rigging one myself turned out to be a tall order.

The site I built with it really did load slowly. Eventually I couldn’t put up with it and switched away. For a while I kept it around purely because it was pretty.

I also wanted an About page built around a BotUI chatbot. I remember spending ages on that, trying one suggestion after another from Google. The JavaScript seemed to do absolutely nothing. Maybe it never loaded in the first place…

For all the tinkering, I still like how Sakura looks. To find the settings now I’d start with the repository guide. The theme has its own settings screen, so plenty of changes are possible without touching the source files. For further styling, the author recommends a child theme.

# Sakurairo

The screenshot is from networkos.club, a site in the official showcase. It’s someone else’s setup, rather than my old site or the default appearance.

Sakurairo is a reworking of Sakura V3. Its manual groups settings by scope, including global options, the home page and individual pages. Having so much in the dashboard would have saved me some of the hunting through tutorials I did with Sakura.

What you can change depends on the version and configuration. Unfortunately I still had the same slow loading when I used it.

# Ashe

The Ashe theme page describes support for personal and multi-author blogs, a large header image, a full-screen slider and a mobile layout. Compared with the first two themes, the photos and posts take centre stage.

If what you want is one lovely big image and a clear list of posts underneath, this one is worth a look.

# Argon

Argon is one I came away liking. You can change the theme colour, choose a one-, two- or three-column layout, and switch to night mode.

The theme documentation is a good place to see what you’d like to configure.

# Hexo

# ShokaX

ShokaX is derived from Shoka. It’s the theme this blog uses.

I’ve changed the styling, so the current site only tells you so much about the default look. I’ve written up the details in my customisation notes and upgrade notes.

# Two more that caught my eye

These two are based on the official material. I haven’t used them in the same way as the ones above.

# Typecho: Joe

Joe has a two-column layout, configurable colours and syntax highlighting. It looks worth considering for a technical blog on Typecho if you like a little more going on around the posts.

# Hexo: Butterfly

Butterfly has a distinct card layout and two columns, with night mode, background effects and mouse-click effects. You can probably see why it appealed to me.

The official demo and docs are a good way to pick out the effects you want.

items.title: Repairing the Ciri Main Menu Background Mod
items.content_html:
I wanted Ciri in Night City – Main Menu Background Replacer to work on Cyberpunk 2077 version 2.0 and later, including the Phantom Liberty logo.

Update 1.1.0: In my 1.0.0 fix, the animations that play when loading a save disappeared. I’ve restored the sequence, although its final shot now uses the replacement main menu background.

The missing logo and missing loading sequence have different causes. The logo disappeared because the mod shipped older textures. The sequence disappeared because of how broadly the original mod replaced the background assets.

If you’re here for the loading animations, skip to the final section. That’s where I rebuild the mod from scratch.

Here’s the original mod at startup. The Phantom Liberty logo is missing:

# Fixing the logo

I used WolvenKit.

# Restore the Phantom Liberty logo

Open Mod Browser and locate the installed mod.

Right-click the base folder and choose Add selected items to project. In Project Explorer, find and delete menu_background.xbm and menu_background_1080p.xbm . These are the two files causing the problem.

# Pack the project

Choose Build → Pack Project. WolvenKit writes a ZIP archive in the project folder. Remove the original mod and install the newly packed version in Cyberpunk 2077. The expansion logo is back:

# How the original mod works

Some background: Reading Cyberpunk 2077’s UI assets.

I took the long way round to figure this out. Here’s what I found along the way.

# Locating the background

The mod changes quite a few files. I started by looking for the actual image it replaced.

The main menu image changes as you progress through the story. I traced the images to base\gameplay\gui\world\loading_screens\ .

Directory names such as loading_screen_5_after_q101 and loading_screen_10_after_q112 seem to correspond to story milestones. For instance, here’s loading_screen_10_after_q112\loading_screen_10_shot_01.xbm :

I recognised that as the background that appears after sneaking in to install the virus on the float. Here’s another example, loading_screen_5_after_q101\loading_screen_5_shot_01.xbm :

It matches the menu in my current save:

# A closer look at the inkwidget

The corresponding .inkwidget seemed the likely place to change the background. The old mod still replaced it successfully, despite the missing logo, so I could use it for comparison.

I focused on loading_screen_5_after_q101.inkwidget because I could compare it with the menu I was actually seeing. The game file is on the left, the modded file on the right:

On the right, the important file is cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 , the replacement Ciri animation. On the left, my background used the first shot, so I set the second and third shots aside.

smoke_loop.bk2 is a looping video of smoke.

shot_01_assets.inkatlas picks out the three light columns ( ad ) and the blinking lights ( antenna_lights ) from the texture.

Here’s the underlying texture, short_01_assets.xbm . You can see the light effects together before the atlas separates them:

loading_screen_5_shot_01.inkatlas supplies the main background. Its four bounds run from 0 to 1, so the selected region covers the entire texture.

On the annotated menu, ① is the smoke loop and ② comes from the shot assets atlas:

For the still image in this particular scene, replacing loading_screen_5_shot_01.xbm would do it.

# Why the mod replaces every widget

Replacing that one texture wouldn’t cover the other stages of the story. Looking more closely, I found that the modded loading_screen_5_after_q101.inkwidget had the same contents as the game’s base\gameplay\gui\world\loading_screens\initial_loading_screen\initial_loading_screen.inkwidget .

The cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 animation referenced by that initial widget had already been replaced with Ciri. Copying the widget into the q101 folder therefore gave that menu the Ciri background as well. The original mod did the same in every corresponding folder. If the game keeps switching backgrounds, why not replace the lot?

# Where the logo fix actually belongs

None of that detective work directly fixed the logo. I couldn’t find a logo in the original q101 widget; what I’d traced was the background replacement. But once I’d accounted for those files, the rest of the mod was much easier to inspect.

Two files stood out under base\gameplay\gui\fullscreen\main_menu\ : menu_background.xbm and menu_background_1080p.xbm . Here’s the modded texture on the left and the game’s on the right:

The game already has the right logo. The mod’s older textures override it. Removing both textures from the mod lets the game use its own copies.

# Update: restoring the loading animations

After fixing the logo, I loaded a save from the main menu. Usually there’s a short sequence that changes with the story. This time the entire load was black.

The sequence has three shots. Here are examples, in playback order:

# Why the sequence went missing

The mod replaced each story-specific widget with initial_loading_screen.inkwidget . Those original widgets also define the loading shots, as described in the inkwidget notes.

In the comparison below, the story widget has ls_01 , ls_02 and ls_03 . The initial widget only has main_menu and loading_screen .

The first remaining entry, main_menu , refers to the replacement Ciri video, cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 . The second refers to a different animation shown on entering the menu. The game can no longer find any of the three shots when loading a save.

# Restore the shots and replace the menu background

I started a fresh project. In Asset Browser I found the original mod’s Ciri background video, listed here as cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 , and added it to the project. Then I located the game’s loading_screen_5_after_q101.inkwidget and initial_loading_screen.inkwidget . I added the former to the project for editing and used Open without adding to project for the latter.

Copy the cp_bg_alpha_faded.bk2 resource from the initial widget into the q101 widget’s externalDependenciesForInternalItems :
